regionData.title: SOUTH POLE
regionData.subtitle: Extreme cold, altitude and polar isolation
regionData.desc: A high-altitude Antarctic research scenario modeled on Amundsen–Scott South Pole Station. The values below describe that reference station, not all of Antarctica.
notes: Severe cold requires layered protection, thermal management and shelter access.
Station elevation creates reduced oxygen partial pressure compared with sea level.
Polar day and polar night can challenge circadian rhythms and sleep.
Weather and seasonal access can constrain emergency evacuation.
sources: USAP — South Pole climate and altitude
NASA — Why the South Pole is colder

regionData.title: HOT DESERT
regionData.subtitle: Heat load, dehydration and airborne dust
regionData.desc: An illustrative hot-desert field mission; day-night temperature and precipitation are biome-level educational references, not observations at a selected coordinate.
notes: Skin/land-surface temperatures can be far above nearby air temperature.
Sweat losses, sun exposure and effort alter physiological heat strain.
Wind-driven dust may reduce visibility and affect respiratory protection.
Water and medical evacuation planning are mission-specific.

regionData.title: EARTHQUAKE ZONE
regionData.subtitle: Shaking, aftershocks and unstable infrastructure
regionData.desc: No fixed quake magnitude or ground acceleration is assigned. Earthquake intensity and secondary hazards change with event, site geology and building conditions.
notes: Shaking intensity is not the same as earthquake magnitude.
Weak sediments can amplify local ground motion.
Liquefaction requires susceptible water-saturated soils.
Assessment and rescue actions must follow actual site safety protocols.

regionData.title: TSUNAMI COAST
regionData.subtitle: Inundation, currents and delayed wave trains
regionData.desc: A tsunami-prone coast has no universal wave height or arrival time. A tsunami can consist of multiple waves and conditions depend on the source and coastal geometry.
facts: Do not assume first is largest
notes: Local sources can leave very little time for official alerts.
Multiple waves may continue for hours; never treat the first wave as the all-clear.
Run-up and flooding differ by coastline and bathymetry.
This prototype does not issue tsunami warnings or route evacuations.

regionData.title: VOLCANIC REGION
regionData.subtitle: Ash, gases and hazardous access corridors
regionData.desc: Volcanic exposure is event-, wind- and distance-dependent. No fixed plume concentration, lava temperature at a site or gas dose is assigned.
notes: Fine ash is abrasive and can disrupt mechanical equipment and engines.
SO₂, CO₂ and other volcanic gases vary with volcanic system and weather.
Protective equipment must be based on measured concentrations.
Evacuation corridors can be affected by ash and lahars.

regionData.title: FLOODPLAIN
regionData.subtitle: Floodwater, precipitation and disrupted logistics
regionData.desc: A floodplain response mission depends on rainfall, watershed, terrain, hydrology and changing local forecasts. Satellite precipitation estimates are not ground-truth water-depth readings.
notes: Satellite rainfall estimates are a monitoring input, not a flood-depth sensor.
Fast-moving water and submerged obstacles can be dangerous.
Water contamination and electrical hazards need separate evaluation.
No live flood forecast or automated rescue routing is provided.
sources: NASA GPM — IMERG and landslide viewer
